Mark leading-NA cells with an explicit state label

Source: R/sequence_terminal.R
mark_first_state.Rd

mark_first_state() fills every missing cell before each sequence's first observed state with an explicit state, "Start" by default, and returns the wide table. It is the counterpart of mark_terminal_state() for left-censored data, such as students who join a course at different times: a network built from the result shows into which states the late entrants arrive. Internal and trailing missing cells are left as they are, and so are rows observed from the first position or not at all.

The marked state is a transient entry point, not an absorbing state: once a sequence leaves it, it never returns. In a transition network built from the result, its row holds the moves from it, which go to the first observed states and, for sequences with two or more leading missing cells, back to itself.

Usage

mark_first_state(data, state = "Start", cols = NULL)

Arguments

data

The sequences: a matrix or data frame with one row per actor and one column per position, holding state labels, with NA for a missing observation. Without cols, the frame must be one column or a numbered run of positions (T1, T2, ...); other columns beside them raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input.

state

The label written into the leading missing cells, a single non-empty string. Default "Start". If the label already occurs in data, a warning of class nestimate_state_collision is given and _1, _2, ... is appended until it is unique, so the marker is never confused with an observed state.

cols

The columns holding the positions, in order; only they are returned. A name not in data raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input. Default NULL (every column).

Value

A data frame of character columns with the shape of data (or of its cols), the leading missing cells filled with the marker. The label used is kept in the "leading_state" attribute, which differs from state when it had to be made unique. The columns are marked as positions, so build_network() reads them without state_cols.

See also

mark_terminal_state(), actor_endpoints()

Examples

M <- mark_first_state(trajectories, state = "Start")
# In a chain built from M, "Start" is a transient entry point.
